transcript.text: Samsung WD90T534DBW washer dryer - clothes are still damp at the end of the wash and dry programme. It's not that old. Is the heater going?

Not necessarily. A failed heater is actually one of the less likely causes, and a heater fault usually produces an error code. Most "damp at the end" complaints on washer dryers like this one come down to load size, settings, or a moisture-removal problem.

## 1. Check the load size (most common cause)
The WD90T534DBW is 9kg wash but only 6kg dry. If you fill it for a wash and then let it carry straight on to drying, it's overloaded for the dry stage. Air can't circulate and the sensor ends the cycle while clothes are still damp.
• For wash + dry in one go, keep the load to 6kg or less, and ideally less for bulky items like towels and jeans.
• If you've washed a full load, take some out before drying.

## 2. Check the dry settings
• Dryness level: if it's set to "Iron Dry" rather than "Cupboard Dry", clothes are meant to come out slightly damp.
• Timed drying: a short time setting may simply not be enough.
• Spin speed: a low spin (e.g. 800) leaves much more water for the dryer to remove. Use the highest spin the fabrics allow.
• Mixed loads: heavy towels mixed with thin items often leave the heavy stuff damp when the sensor decides the load is done.

## 3. Check moisture removal
This is a condenser washer dryer. It uses cold water to condense the steam and pumps it away, so:
• Clean the debris/drain filter (small hatch at the bottom front). A blocked filter is a classic cause of poor drying.
• Make sure the water supply is fully on and the drain hose isn't kinked.
• Lint build-up in the drying duct and condenser can restrict airflow. Running Drum Clean regularly helps. Heavy fluff build-up inside the ductwork may need an engineer.

## 4. How to tell if it's actually the heater
Run a dry-only programme with a small load (2–3 hand towels) and check partway through:
• Clothes and door glass warm, but clothes still damp: the heater is working. The problem is airflow, condensing, or the filter.
• Everything stone cold after 20–30 minutes: suspect the drying heater, a thermal fuse/thermostat, or the fan.
• An error code on the display, such as HE/HC-type heating codes or a fan code: note it down, check the manual, and you'll have a definite fault to report.

## 5. If it does turn out to be a fault
• Warranty: Samsung's standard warranty is usually 1 year, though many retailers and promotions extend this. Check your paperwork.
• Out of warranty: in the UK, the Consumer Rights Act lets you claim against the retailer if goods don't last a reasonable time (up to 6 years in England and Wales, 5 in Scotland). Expect to have to show the fault isn't down to misuse once it's past 6 months. A machine only a few years old with a heater failure is a reasonable case to raise with the retailer.

If you tell me roughly how big the loads are, which dry setting you use, and whether the clothes come out warm or cold, I can help narrow it down further.
Loads are a full 9kg drum, washed and dried in one go. I use Cupboard Dry, and the clothes come out hot and damp, not cold. The manual does say 6kg for drying, I think.

That pretty much solves it: the heater is fine, and the load is the problem.

Hot clothes mean the heater is working. Damp clothes after a full 9kg wash-and-dry mean the machine is drying about 50% more than it's designed to. Wet clothes are packed too tightly for hot air to circulate, so the outer layers heat up while the middle stays damp. The moisture sensor can also end the cycle early because it's reading the drier items on the outside.

## What to do

Option 1: Wash full, dry in two batches
• Wash your 9kg load as normal.
• Take out at least a third (roughly 3kg or more) before drying.
• Dry the rest, then dry the removed portion separately.

Option 2: Wash smaller loads
• If you want true one-step wash and dry, load no more than 6kg.
• For bulky items like towels, jeans, and bedding, go lighter still, around 4-5kg. Heavy, thick fabrics hold a lot of water and need more room.

Rough weight guide (dry clothes):
• Bath towel: ~0.6-0.7kg
• Pair of jeans: ~0.6-0.8kg
• Double duvet cover: ~1kg
• T-shirt: ~0.15-0.2kg

## A few extras that help
• Use the highest spin speed the fabrics allow, so less water is left for the dryer to remove.
• Separate heavy and light items where you can. Towels and jeans dry better together than mixed with thin shirts.
• Clean the drain filter at the bottom front if you haven't recently. It's quick and helps drying.

## If it's still damp with a proper load
Try one cycle with 6kg or less. If clothes still come out hot and damp, then look at:
• Water supply fully on (it needs cold water to condense the steam)
• Drain hose not kinked or blocked
• Lint build-up in the condenser or duct, which may need an engineer

But with 9kg in a 6kg dryer, overloading is almost certainly the cause.
